No slides were given for this lecture. The notes of Alessa, Alsalamah and Alomar word for word, in their own order (green), every gift (red) under the part it belongs to and the Aldughaither summary (grey, at the end).

Notes

Day-Surgery Pathway

Preoperative assessment → patient classified as:

Fit for surgery
Unsuitable for day surgery
Requires optimization before proceeding
Once optimized/cleared by anesthesia → patient attends on day of surgery, undergoes the procedure, receives postoperative medications/instructions, then is discharged. Follow-up may be by telephone or in-person review.
  • Before a day-surgery open hernia repair, the service that must assess the patient is Anesthesia. 437 ×3
Notes

Patient Selection

3 MAJOR QUESTIONS
1 Is the operation appropriate for day surgery?
2 Is there anything that would be done by keeping the patient overnight that cannot safely be done at home? 3 Are the patient's home/social circumstances adequate for same-day discharge?

Selection depends on surgical factors, medical factors, and social factors.

The 3 major questions: (1) Is the operation appropriate for day surgery? (2) Is there anything done by keeping the patient overnight that cannot safely be done at home? (3) Are the home/social circumstances adequate for same-day discharge?
Notes

Surgical Factors

Low risk of major postoperative complications — high-risk surgery generally not suitable
Should not require prolonged specialized postoperative care/observation
Abdominal/thoracic procedures should generally use minimally invasive techniques (e.g. laparoscopy)
Postoperative pain must be controllable with oral analgesia ± local/regional anesthesia
Rapid expected return to oral intake, safe mobilization, and usual functional status
Some urgent procedures may still be performed as day surgery, e.g. incision/drainage of an abscess.
  • Not suitable for day surgery: reversal of ileostomy (bowel anastomosis → needs admission to watch return of bowel function/leak). 438 ×2
  • Total mastectomy was keyed as a possible day-case procedure (total thyroidectomy, carotid endarterectomy and ileostomy reversal are not). 436
Notes

Medical Factors

Fitness for day surgery should be determined by functional assessment during preoperative evaluation, rather than age alone.
FactorConsideration
Stable chronic diseaseAcceptable if adequately controlled preoperatively (e.g. diabetes, asthma, hypertension) — day surgery may reduce interruption of regular medications
Unstable medical conditionsGenerally inappropriate — e.g. unstable blood glucose/diabetes, uncontrolled blood pressure, other clinically unstable disease
ObesityMay increase perioperative risk: reduced mobility, respiratory/breathing problems, increased complications
ELDERLY PATIENTS
Chronological age alone should not determine eligibility. Suitability depends more on functional status and comorbidities — a younger patient with multiple comorbidities may be less suitable than a healthy older patient.
  • After a day-case lap cholecystectomy the patient was admitted to the ward — what to assess post-op: cardio-respiratory assessment. 434 ×2
Notes

Social Factors

Patient should have:

Responsible adult/caregiver available for ~24h after discharge
Access to a telephone
Reasonable geographical proximity to the hospital
Adequate understanding of the procedure and postoperative requirements
Motivation, education, and engagement with the pathway and consent process
⭐ EXAM IMPORTANT A patient medically suitable for day surgery but living 4 hours away from the hospital → not suitable, because social/geographical factors are part of patient selection. Eligibility is determined by the whole clinical + social picture, not one isolated factor such as age.
  • Obese day-surgery patient rated "low to intermediate risk" → the reason is the BMI (32). 436
⭐ Exam: a patient medically suitable for day surgery but living 4 hours away from the hospital → not suitable. Social/geographical factors are part of selection; eligibility is the whole picture, not one factor such as age.
  • Social factors = access to a phone, the area they live in, education; "access to a public area" is not a criterion. 438 436
Notes

Patient Preparation & Education

Patients/caregivers should receive clear and detailed information about:

Planned procedure
Expected perioperative course
Preparation before surgery
Postoperative care
Medications
Discharge instructions
When/how to seek medical help
Adequate education allows patients to make informed decisions and improves safe participation in the day-surgery pathway.
Notes

Anesthetic Management

MAIN AIM
Use an anesthetic technique allowing rapid recovery and safe early discharge. The anesthetist should identify relevant anesthetic risks and factors that may delay discharge.

Prefer drugs with rapid onset and offset. Avoid long-acting anesthetic/sedative drugs because residual effects may delay recovery, delay mobilization, and prevent safe discharge.

PONV
Aim to minimize postoperative nausea and vomiting because it is a common cause of delayed discharge. Use anesthetic/analgesic techniques that preserve or allow rapid recovery of normal function.
Notes

Postoperative Analgesia

Prefer regular oral analgesia
Often combine with long-acting NSAIDs, if not contraindicated
Supplement with local or regional anesthesia/nerve blocks where appropriate
Regional/local techniques reduce postoperative pain and may reduce systemic analgesic requirements.
Notes

Recovery & Discharge

Discharge can be nurse-led once predefined discharge criteria/milestones are met. Discharge planning should begin before the operation, with medications and instructions arranged in advance.

Patient discharged only after:

Required recovery milestones achieved
Adequate pain control
Appropriate recovery from anesthesia
Safe mobilization/functional recovery
Required instructions provided
Notes

At Discharge

PATIENT SHOULD RECEIVE
Discharge summary
Prescribed medications
Written postoperative instructions
Information on expected symptoms and complications
Clear criteria for when to return to hospital
Telephone/contact number for problems after discharge

Access to an appropriately trained/senior healthcare professional capable of giving postoperative advice, assessing reported problems, and advising whether hospital reassessment/readmission is required.

  • Before discharge after a simple hemorrhoidectomy → appropriate analgesia with written instructions. 437 ×5
  • Discharge needs a summary (with overnight medical help if needed), analgesia with written instructions, clinic follow-up — NOT "follow-up in the emergency department". 438
Notes

High-Yield Day-Surgery Principle

CORE FORMULA
Successful day surgery = appropriate procedure + medically stable patient + suitable home/social support + effective short- acting anesthesia/analgesia + safe discharge and follow-up.
Successful day surgery = appropriate procedure + medically stable patient + suitable home/social support + short-acting anesthesia/analgesia + safe discharge and follow-up.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 Patient selection rests on 3 questions: is the operation appropriate, does anything require overnight admission, and are home/social circumstances adequate
2 Some urgent procedures (e.g. abscess I&D) can still be appropriate for day surgery
3 Stable chronic disease is acceptable if controlled; unstable disease (uncontrolled glucose/BP) is generally disqualifying
4 Functional status and comorbidities determine elderly suitability, not chronological age — a younger patient with more comorbidities may be less suitable than a healthy older one
5 ⭐ A medically fit patient can still be unsuitable for day surgery on social/geographical grounds alone (e.g. living 4 hours from hospital) — eligibility is the whole picture, not one factor
6 Anesthetic choice favors rapid onset/offset drugs; long-acting sedatives risk delayed recovery, mobilization, and discharge
7 PONV is a leading cause of delayed discharge and must be actively minimized
8 Postoperative analgesia favors oral ± long-acting NSAIDs ± regional/local blocks over strategies causing prolonged sedation
9 Discharge is nurse-led once criteria/milestones are met, not once a set number of hours has passed
10 Discharge planning starts before the operation — medications and instructions should be arranged in advance
11 Every discharged patient needs a discharge summary, medications, written instructions, red-flag criteria, and a contact number staffed by someone able to advise on readmission
  • Carotid endarterectomy requires in-hospital admission (stroke, neck hematoma, BP instability). 437 ×5
